title: Balance new features with technical health
summary: Shortcuts in code, known as technical debt, slow the team down over time. A good PM makes room for fixing them, so the team can keep delivering at speed.

beginner: Ask the engineers which parts of the system slow them down or break most often.
Ask what each problem costs: slower delivery, more bugs, outages or security risk.
Agree a regular share of capacity for technical health, often 15 to 25 percent.
Put technical health items in the same backlog and prioritise them openly.
Explain the business value of this work to stakeholders in plain terms.
intermediate: Build a list of technical debt with the team, sorted by cost and risk.
Agree a standing share of capacity and track it.
Prioritise debt alongside features using the same criteria.
Report the benefit in delivery speed and reliability.
experienced: Separate deliberate, sensible debt from reckless debt, and set rules for each.
Tie technical health to measures such as lead time, failed changes and incidents.
Fund larger platform or architecture work through the roadmap, not just spare capacity.
Make technical health a shared goal for product and engineering leaders.

canDelegateTo.task: List the debt and estimate its cost and risk
Supply data on incidents and failed releases

toolExamples.jira: Label technical health items and track the share of each sprint spent on them.
toolExamples.github: Use code scanning and dependency alerts to spot health risks.
toolExamples.gitlab: Use code quality reports to show where health is getting worse.

definitionOfDone: Technical debt list agreed with the team
pitfalls: Treating all technical work as optional
Big rewrites with no plan to deliver value along the way

leaderView.good: Teams make steady room for fixing technical debt, and can explain the trade-off.
ask: How much time do we spend on technical health, and is it enough?
What's slowing the team down most?
signs: Technical debt is only discussed in a crisis.
Delivery is getting slower each quarter.
